parts.problemMd:

parts.solutionMd:

A student uses the data in Figure 1.1 to make two conclusions:

- February is always the wettest month in Finland.
- The temperature in October is always higher than the temperature in November in Finland.

Explain these limitations.
parts.solutionMd:
Limitation 1: The data come from one farm, so they may not represent the whole of Finland  **[1 mark]**.

Explanation 1: Other parts of Finland have different temperatures and precipitation, so the pattern could be different there  **[1 mark]**.

Limitation 2: The data are mean values, so they do not show what happens in each year  **[1 mark]**.

Explanation 2: Weather varies from year to year, so in some years November could be warmer than October  **[1 mark]**.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This answer is assessed using a point-marked approach.
> 
> - **One mark** for each limitation and **one mark** for its matching explanation, to a maximum of 4 marks
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of how to respond to this question. Other information that could be used includes:
> 
> - The climate is changing, so past data may not show future patterns
> - The conclusions say 'always', which one set of data cannot prove

> - Any other suitable response

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Each explanation must match its limitation. Write the explanation straight after the limitation so the examiner can see they belong together.

parts.problemMd:
A scientist wants to use a random sampling strategy to estimate the population of giant African land snails in Florida.

Describe a random sampling strategy to estimate the population of giant African land snails in Florida.

In your answer include a method to:

- select the area to sample
- collect and record your data
- estimate the population of giant African land snails in Florida.
parts.solutionMd:
Put a grid over a map of Florida  **[1 mark]** and use a random number generator to choose grid squares to sample  **[1 mark]**. At each site, place a 1 m² quadrat and count the snails inside it  **[1 mark]**, recording each count in a tally table  **[1 mark]**. Repeat this for at least 50 quadrats, then multiply the mean number of snails per m² by the area of Florida  **[1 mark]**.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This answer is assessed using a point-marked approach.
> 
> - **One mark** for each valid point, to a maximum of 5 marks
> - You must cover all three bullet points to gain 5 marks
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of how to respond to this question. Other information that could be used includes:
> 
> - Use GPS coordinates to find the sampling sites
> - Repeat the sampling on several days and use the mean
> - Any other suitable response
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> - Describing systematic sampling, for example sampling at regular intervals, when the question asks for random sampling
> - Forgetting to repeat the sampling

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Use the three bullets as headings in your plan and give at least one point under each.
> - Do not copy the question into your answer. Start straight away with what you would do.

parts.problemMd:
Scientists predict that the mean global temperature will increase.

One group of scientists predicts that the mean global temperature in 2033 will increase by 1.5 °C and that the mean global temperature in 2100 will increase by 5.4 °C.

Calculate the mean annual increase in global temperature between 2033 and 2100.

Give your answer to two significant figures.
parts.solutionMd:
Temperature increase: 5.4 - 1.5 = 3.9 °C  **[1 mark]**

Number of years: 2100 - 2033 = 67

Mean annual increase: 3.9 ÷ 67 = 0.0582... °C  **[1 mark]**

To two significant figures: **0.058 °C**  **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Zeros at the start of a decimal are not significant, so the first two significant figures of 0.0582 are 5 and 8.
> - Show every step of your working. If the final answer is wrong, you can still gain marks for correct working.

parts.problemMd:
Scientists predict that the mean global temperature will increase.

Most scientists predict global temperature change as a range of values.

Suggest two reasons why a range of temperatures is predicted and not an actual value.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Any **two** from:
> 
> - The predictions are based on variable or uncertain data
> - The calculations are not precise
> - Scientists do not know how energy use will change in the future
> - Scientists cannot predict how the human population will change
> - There may be natural changes in climate
> - Current trends may only be short term
> 
> **[2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
A scientist wants to predict the global production of carbon dioxide from manufacturing cement in 2040.

The scientist states:

"700 thousand million tonnes of carbon dioxide were produced in 2000.

1600 thousand million tonnes of carbon dioxide were produced in 2020."

The scientist uses this data to predict there will be 2300 thousand million tonnes of carbon dioxide produced in 2040.

Suggest two reasons why this prediction may not be the actual value of carbon dioxide produced in 2040.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Any **two** from:
> 
> - The population may change, which changes the demand for buildings
> - The rate of cement production may change
> - Other building materials may be developed
> - New technologies may reduce the carbon dioxide released
> 
> **[2 marks]**

parts.problemMd:
Increased carbon dioxide concentrations in the atmosphere contribute to climate change.

One strategy for managing the impacts of climate change is climate change adaptation.

State what is meant by climate change adaptation.
parts.solutionMd:
**Changing behaviour, practices or infrastructure to cope with the impacts of climate change**  **[1 mark]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Adaptation means coping with the effects of climate change. Cutting carbon dioxide emissions is mitigation, which is a different strategy.

parts.problemMd:
Increased carbon dioxide concentrations in the atmosphere contribute to climate change.

One strategy for managing the impacts of climate change is climate change adaptation.

Describe two examples of climate change adaptation.
parts.solutionMd:
Farmers grow drought-resistant crops that can survive hotter and drier conditions  **[1 mark]**.

Coastal towns build stronger flood defences, such as sea walls, to protect against rising sea levels  **[1 mark]**.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - **One mark** for each described example, to a maximum of 2 marks
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of how to respond to this question. Other information that could be used includes:
> 
> - Laws that stop new buildings on floodplains or near coasts
> - Changing building designs and materials to cope with heat or flooding
> - Studying local risks so that communities can prepare
> - Any other suitable response
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> - Giving a way to reduce carbon dioxide emissions, which is mitigation, not adaptation

parts.problemMd:
Figure 5.1 shows the global production of non-biodegradable bioplastics and biodegradable bioplastics in 2021 and 2023.

![Stacked bar chart of global production of non-biodegradable and biodegradable bioplastics: 2021 totals 1,800 thousand tonnes and 2023 totals 2,400. The 2025 bar is blank for plotting. y-axis 0–5,000 thousand tonnes.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-environmental-management-25/water/plastic-pollution/assets/001-stacked-bar-chart-of-global-production-of-non-bi.png)

*Figure 5.1*

Table 5.1 shows the predicted global production of non-biodegradable bioplastics and biodegradable bioplastics in 2025.

**Table 5.1**

| year | global production of non-biodegradable bioplastics / thousand tonnes | global production of biodegradable bioplastics / thousand tonnes |
|---|---|---|
| 2025 | 2500 | 2400 |

Plot the data for 2025 on the grid in Figure 5.1.
parts.solutionMd:
Draw a stacked bar for 2025. The biodegradable section goes from 0 to 2400 thousand tonnes, and the non-biodegradable section sits on top of it, from 2400 to 4900 thousand tonnes  **[1 mark]**.

Shade each section to match the key and draw the bar the same width as the 2021 and 2023 bars  **[1 mark]**.

> **[exam-tip]**
> - This is a stacked bar chart, so the top of the bar shows the total: 2400 + 2500 = 4900. Plotting the non-biodegradable section from 0 to 2500 is a common mistake.

parts.problemMd:
Figure 5.1 shows the global production of non-biodegradable bioplastics and biodegradable bioplastics in 2021 and 2023.

![Stacked bar chart of global production of non-biodegradable and biodegradable bioplastics: 2021 totals 1,800 thousand tonnes and 2023 totals 2,400. The 2025 bar is blank for plotting. y-axis 0–5,000 thousand tonnes.](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SyllabAI/syllabai-resources/0fe5f77210f74aaeb3f6c491dfe0263d12db738c/SME-ExamQuestion/cie-igcse-environmental-management-25/water/plastic-pollution/assets/001-stacked-bar-chart-of-global-production-of-non-bi.png)

*Figure 5.1*

Determine the mass of non-biodegradable bioplastics produced in 2023.

Give the unit.
parts.solutionMd:
Top of the 2023 bar = 2400 thousand tonnes and top of the biodegradable section = 1300 thousand tonnes  **[1 mark]**

2400 - 1300 = **1100**  **[1 mark]**

Unit: **thousand tonnes**  **[1 mark]**

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - **One mark** for reading both values from the graph
> - **One mark** for the subtraction
> - **One mark** for a unit that matches your value: 1100 thousand tonnes or 1 100 000 tonnes

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Read the non-biodegradable section as the difference between two readings, not as the top of the bar.

parts.problemMd:
Biodegradable bioplastics break down over time.

Name one group of organisms that break down biodegradable bioplastics.
parts.solutionMd:
**Bacteria**  **[1 mark]**

Fungi are also accepted.

parts.problemMd:
Biodegradable bioplastics break down over time.

Name two products formed when biodegradable bioplastics break down.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Unnamed 'gases' are not credited.
> 
> Any **two** from:
> 
> - Water
> - Biomass
> - Carbon dioxide
> - Methane
> 
> **[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Name the gas. 'Gases' on its own does not score, but 'carbon dioxide' or 'methane' does.

parts.problemMd:
Biodegradable bioplastics break down over time.

Suggest two abiotic factors that affect the rate of break down of biodegradable bioplastics.
parts.solutionMd:
> **[mark-scheme]**
> Any **two** from:
> 
> - Temperature
> - Water (moisture)
> - Soil pH
> - Oxygen
> - Salinity
> - Light
> 
> **[2 marks]**

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Abiotic means non-living. Living factors such as the number of bacteria are biotic, so they do not score here.

parts.problemMd:
Bioaccumulation and biomagnification are two impacts of plastic pollution on marine ecosystems.

Describe other impacts of plastic pollution on marine ecosystems.
parts.solutionMd:
Animals such as turtles and seabirds become entangled in plastic  **[1 mark]**, so they cannot swim or feed properly  **[1 mark]**. Animals mistake floating plastic for food  **[1 mark]**, which blocks their digestive system and can cause starvation  **[1 mark]**.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This answer is assessed using a point-marked approach.
> 
> - One mark for each valid point
> - Maximum 4 marks
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of how to respond to this question. Other information that could be used includes:
> 
> - Floating plastic and litter on beaches cause visual pollution
> - People may stop using polluted beaches and coastal waters
> - Any other suitable response
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> - Repeating bioaccumulation or biomagnification, which the question has already given
> - Writing 'it causes pollution' without saying what the plastic does

> **[exam-tip]**
> - For a four-mark 'describe', give an impact and then say what it does to the animal. Each impact plus its effect can earn two marks.

parts.problemMd:
Suggest how planting trees affects interception.

Give a reason for your answer.
parts.solutionMd:
Planting trees increases interception  **[1 mark]** because there are more leaves to catch the rain before it reaches the ground  **[1 mark]**.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> - **One mark** for the effect: interception increases
> - **One mark** for a reason linked to the effect, for example more leaves and branches to catch rain

> **[exam-tip]**
> - The question asks for an effect and a reason, so give both. Start with the direction of change (increases), then explain it.

parts.problemMd:
The oceans are a store of water.

Desalination makes sea water potable.

Define potable water.
parts.solutionMd: **Water that is safe to drink**  **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd:
Distillation is one type of desalination.

Describe the process of distillation.
parts.solutionMd:
The sea water is heated until it boils  **[1 mark]**. The salt stays behind in the liquid  **[1 mark]**. The steam is cooled so that it condenses into pure water  **[1 mark]**.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This answer is assessed using a point-marked approach.
> 
> - **One mark** for heating the water until it boils
> - **One mark** each for any two further steps, to a maximum of 3 marks
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of how to respond to this question. Other information that could be used includes:
> 
> - The steam is pure water because the salt does not evaporate
> - Any other suitable response

parts.problemMd:
Distillation is one type of desalination.

Name one other type of desalination.
parts.solutionMd: **Reverse osmosis**  **[1 mark]**

parts.problemMd: Discuss the benefits and limitations of desalination.
parts.solutionMd:
Desalination increases the amount of fresh water available  **[1 mark]** because it uses sea water, which is not drinkable  **[1 mark]**. It can supply water for irrigating crops in dry areas  **[1 mark]**.

However, desalination plants are expensive to build, so the water costs more per litre than water from rivers or aquifers  **[1 mark]**. They also use large amounts of energy; if this comes from fossil fuels, it adds to carbon dioxide emissions and climate change  **[1 mark]**. They produce salty brine, which can harm marine ecosystems when it is released back into the sea  **[1 mark]**.

> **[mark-scheme]**
> **Mark allocation**
> 
> This answer is assessed using a point-marked approach.
> 
> - **One mark** for each valid benefit or limitation, to a maximum of 6 marks
> - A maximum of **5 marks** for benefits and a maximum of **5 marks** for limitations, so you must cover both sides to gain full marks
> 
> **Alternative content**
> 
> The answer above is just one example of how to respond to this question. Other information that could be used includes:
> 
> - Desalination produces very pure water
> - It removes bacteria and other pathogens
> - It can reduce the risk of conflict over water supplies
> - Landlocked countries cannot use it
> - Some people are reluctant to drink desalinated water because of its taste
> - Any other suitable response
> 
> **Common errors**
> 
> - Writing 'it is expensive' without saying why, for example the cost of building the plant or the cost per litre
> - Mentioning climate change without linking it to the energy the plant uses
> - Writing only benefits or only limitations

> **[exam-tip]**
> - Plan for at least two points on each side before you start writing.
> - Make every limitation specific. Say what is expensive and why, and link any climate change point to the energy the plant uses.
